questions.stem: A program has 10 crew-months next year. Must-do M1 needs 4 of them whichever of its two start years it uses; must-do M2 needs 3 if it starts next year and none if it starts the year after. A discretionary start needs 7. What follows from this row alone?

options.text: Left free, since 7 fits within the row's 10 crew-months
options.says: The must-dos use part of the row in every plan: M1 always takes 4, so at most 6 remain for anything else.

options.text: Left free, since M2 may start the year after instead
options.says: That is why M2 counts 0 in the floor; M1 still takes 4 in every plan, leaving 6, and 7 does not fit.

options.text: Fixed at 0, since 7 exceeds the 6 the must-dos leave
options.says: Right: the floor is M1's 4 plus M2's smallest use, 0, so the room is 6 and a start needing 7 is in no allowed plan.

options.text: Fixed at 1, since a start that fits must be taken
options.says: A capacity row can only rule a start out; and 7 does not fit in the 6 the must-dos leave.

origin.section: A Row Leaves Each Variable Only What the Others Must Use

questions.stem: Four starts conflict two by two. A colleague wrote the six pair rows; you wrote one row over all four. At an LP point that sets each of the four to 0.4, which rows hold?

options.text: Each pair row holds, and the single row is broken: it sums to 1.6
options.says: Right: each pair sums to 0.8, at most 1, while the four together sum to 1.6, above 1. The single row cuts the point off.

options.text: Each pair row is broken, and the single row holds at 0.4
options.says: A pair sums to 0.4 + 0.4 = 0.8, within its limit of 1; the single row adds all four values.

options.text: Each pair row holds, and the single row holds as well
options.says: The single row adds all four: 1.6 is above 1. Lesson 6.1.3's five projects at 0.5 are the same effect.

options.text: Each pair row is broken, and the single row is broken too
options.says: 0.4 + 0.4 = 0.8 satisfies every pair row; only the single row sees the four together.

origin.section: A Clique of Conflicts Is One Valid Row, Stronger Than Its Pairs

questions.stem: A script derives 40 clique rows for a model. With all of them added, the MILP optimum is the same as before. What does that result show about the 40 rows?

options.text: Each of them is valid, since a wrong one would have to lower the optimum
options.says: A wrong row that cuts off only worse plans leaves the optimum where it was; the page checks every allowed plan on tiny for that reason.

options.text: Each of them keeps this optimum; the check says nothing about worse plans
options.says: Right: an unchanged optimum is a check on the plans near the top only, which is why the brute force over tiny's plans is kept as well.

options.text: Each of them is redundant, since the solver's answer did not change
options.says: Valid rows always leave the optimum unchanged; they can still lower the LP bound, as 19 clique rows did on GridCap small.

options.text: Each of them can be dropped again, since rows that keep the optimum do no work
options.says: The clique rows left the optimum at 22,741 and still lowered the LP bound from 25,170.51 to 24,580.01; keeping the optimum is not doing no work.

origin.section: A Derived Row Is Trusted Only After It Is Checked Against Whole Plans
